title: Inventory Agreement & Pronouns
description: Edit agreement and pronoun problems without being distracted by nearby nouns.
subject: rla
passage:
At the end of each month, a small electronics shop prepares an inventory report. The report lists items that are running low, equipment that needs repair, and supplies that should be reordered. Because several employees contribute notes, the final draft often contains agreement and pronoun problems that are easy to miss during a quick read.

The store manager reminds the team that the grammatical subject controls the verb even when another noun appears closer to it. Phrases such as “along with the spare cables” or “of the replacement parts” can distract an editor from the true subject. Compound subjects and indefinite pronouns require attention as well because they do not always follow the pattern a reader expects from casual speech.

Pronouns create a different problem. A pronoun must clearly refer to the intended noun, and its form must fit its job in the sentence. If two possible nouns appear before “it” or “they,” the sentence may need to be rewritten rather than merely corrected for number. The team’s goal is simple: a reader should never have to stop and guess who completed an action, which item is being discussed, or whether the verb belongs with a nearby distractor instead of the actual subject.

questions.prompt: The box of replacement cables {{blank}} beside the service counter.
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'box,' so 'is' agrees with it.
questions.rule: Cross out interrupting prepositional phrases before matching subject and verb.

options.whyWrong: 'Cables' is inside a prepositional phrase; it is not the subject.
This plural verb phrase does not agree with the singular subject 'box'.
This changes both number and tense without support from the sentence.

questions.prompt: Neither of the two scanners {{blank}} working correctly today.
questions.explanation: 'Neither' is the grammatical subject and takes the singular verb 'is'.
questions.rule: With neither/either, find the actual subject instead of matching the nearest plural noun.

options.whyWrong: 'Neither' is singular in this construction even though 'scanners' is plural.
This shifts the sentence to past tense and still misses the singular subject.
'Have' is plural and does not agree with 'neither'.

questions.prompt: Maya asked Jordan and {{blank}} to verify the count.
questions.explanation: 'Me' is the object form required after 'asked'.
questions.rule: Remove the other name: 'Maya asked me' makes the correct case easier to hear.

options.whyWrong: After the verb 'asked,' the pronoun is an object, so the subject form 'I' is incorrect.
'My' is possessive and must modify a noun.
'Mine' is possessive and does not serve as the object of 'asked' here.

questions.prompt: Choose the clearest revision: “When Leo placed the tablet beside the charger, it was damaged.”
questions.explanation: Naming the damaged item removes the ambiguous pronoun reference.
questions.rule: If a pronoun could point to two nouns, rewrite with the exact noun rather than guessing.

options.text: When Leo placed the tablet beside the charger, it was damaged.
options.whyWrong: 'It' could refer to either the tablet or the charger.

options.text: Leo placed the damaged tablet beside the charger.
When Leo placed it beside it, the damage was visible.
options.whyWrong: Replacing both nouns with pronouns makes the reference even less clear.

options.text: The tablet and charger were beside it when Leo noticed damage.
options.whyWrong: 'It' still lacks a clear antecedent.

questions.prompt: The manager, together with two assistants, {{blank}} the final inventory.
questions.explanation: The true subject is 'manager,' so the singular verb 'reviews' is correct.
questions.rule: Phrases beginning with together with, along with, or as well as do not change the subject.

options.whyWrong: The phrase 'together with two assistants' does not make the singular subject plural.
This plural verb does not agree with the singular subject 'manager'.
This plural past-progressive form changes both agreement and tense.

questions.prompt: Each technician should record {{blank}} own inspection notes before leaving.
questions.explanation: Singular 'they/their' is standard and clearly refers back to 'each technician'.
questions.rule: Make pronouns agree in person and reference; singular they is acceptable in standard English.

options.whyWrong: 'Our' changes the person and does not refer to 'each technician'.
'Your' addresses the reader instead of referring back to the third-person subject.
'Its' is normally used for things or organizations, not a person in this context.

questions.prompt: The invoices and the repair log {{blank}} stored in the locked cabinet.
questions.explanation: The compound subject 'invoices and repair log' is plural, so it takes 'are'.
questions.rule: Subjects joined by and are usually plural unless they name one combined thing.

options.whyWrong: Two nouns joined by 'and' form a plural subject here.
This singular verb phrase does not agree with the compound subject.
The singular past-tense verb does not match the plural subject.

questions.prompt: Either the supervisors or the store manager {{blank}} the closing report tonight.
questions.explanation: With subjects joined by either/or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'store manager'.
questions.rule: For either/or and neither/nor, check the subject closest to the verb.

options.whyWrong: With either/or, the verb normally agrees with the nearer subject; 'manager' is singular.
This plural verb does not agree with the nearer singular subject.
This changes tense and uses plural agreement.
